title: bhakti: the Gita Govinda
hook: Radha waits all night in the place they agreed on, and at dawn he finally turns up

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti in the friend's report, moonlight and sandal paste burning Radha. The same moon, without him.

The plan was simple: meet in the bower by the river, tonight. Radha goes. She waits. The moon comes up over the forest, and he doesn't come. She hears a leaf move and thinks it's him. It isn't. The whole night goes by like that. Then, at dawn, there he is, walking up through the trees with the look of someone who hasn't slept. Before he can say a word, she knows where he's been. What does a devotee, in a poem about God, say to God at a moment like this? Jayadeva gives her the floor.
screen: `MEET IN THE BOWER TONIGHT.` → `THE MOON RISES. NO ONE.` → `AT DAWN, THERE HE IS.`

segments.voice: The poem lingers on what she sees, in paraphrase. His eyes are red from a night without sleep. There are marks on him, traces left by someone else. And her song has a refrain sharp enough to sting: go, Madhava, go, Keshava. Don't speak your deceiving words. Go to the one who kept you up all night. She doesn't soften it or pretend to be fine. And the poem doesn't correct her, not yet. It lets her anger stand on the page, in front of the one the poem calls Lord. Vaishnava poetics has a name for this loving anger: mana, the wounded pride of a lover who knows her worth. It's treated as one of love's real moods, not a fault to hide. Read, as some devotees read it, with Radha as the soul, the scene suggests that bhakti doesn't have to be polite. A devotee may come before God disappointed, even furious, and the relationship holds. In the poem it more than holds: Krishna won't stop seeking her. Later, her friend will gently tell her she's held on long enough. But first, the poem gives her this. An honest complaint is itself a way of staying in the room. Indifference would say nothing. Radha says everything. And Jayadeva, who signs the song as his offering, lets her.
screen: `RED EYES. MARKS. NO SLEEP.` · `GO, MADHAVA. GO, KESHAVA.` · `MANA: LOVE'S WOUNDED PRIDE.` · `THE COMPLAINT KEEPS HER IN THE ROOM.` · then, large: `DON'T SPEAK YOUR DECEIVING WORDS.`

segments.voice: Let the shoulders drop and bring to mind one disappointment you've been carrying quietly, with a person, with life, or with God, if God is part of your life. Don't argue it away or make it bigger; just name it to yourself, plainly, the way Radha does, and notice that you're still here, still facing it. If you pray, bring it into your prayer just as it is; if you don't, let it be said inside, and keep breathing.
Bhakti. Devotion. In the Gita Govinda it has room for mana, love's honest anger, which still keeps facing the beloved.
Your line: go, Madhava, go, Keshava. Even her go-away kept her facing him. That's day nine hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: In Vaishnava devotional performance, Radha's mana, her loving anger, is a recognized mood: singers and Odissi or Bharatanatyam dancers perform her song of dismissal at dawn as part of the Gita Govinda's story of separation and reunion.

fork.reveal: she tells him to go: don't speak your deceiving words. the poem lets her say it all, and Krishna keeps seeking her anyway.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: mana, here the wounded pride of a lover. In Vaishnava poetry it is Radha's mood of loving anger.

trapdoor: what you thought: devotion means always speaking sweetly to God.
what it means: the Gita Govinda gives Radha a song sending Krishna away at dawn, and treats her anger as part of love.
what a scholar hears: Vaishnava poetics names this mood mana, and the dawn scene follows the convention of the wronged lover in Sanskrit poetry.

chat.says: Isn't it wrong for Radha to tell Krishna to go away, if he's God?
options: In the poem her honest anger is part of love; it keeps her facing him.
Yes, and the poem quickly corrects her and makes her apologize first.
It's fine because, in this scene, Krishna is no longer treated as Lord.
chat.meaning: Vaishnava poetics names this mood mana, love's wounded pride. The poem lets Radha's anger stand, and Krishna keeps seeking her.

'Mana' as a named mood in Vaishnava poetics (and the khandita convention in Sanskrit poetics): confirm terminology.
